[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Series and DataFrame Architecture in Pandas"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Pandas is built around two primary data structures: the Series and the DataFrame. Understanding their underlying architecture is crucial for writing efficient, vectorized data manipulation code in Python."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"Anatomy of a Pandas Series"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"A Pandas Series is a one-dimensional labeled array capable of holding data of any type (integer, string, float, python objects, etc.). The axis labels are collectively referred to as the index."},{"order":5,"type":"code","text":"import pandas as pd

# Creating a basic Series
s = pd.Series([10, 20, 30, 40], index=['a', 'b', 'c', 'd'])
print(s)"},{"order":6,"type":"paragraph","text":"Under the hood, a Series consists of three main internal components: an array of actual data (values), an index, and a name. The data is stored as a NumPy ndarray, which guarantees high performance and contiguous memory allocation."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Anatomy of a Pandas DataFrame"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"A DataFrame is a two-dimensional labeled data structure with columns of potentially different types. You can think of it as a container of Series objects that share a common index."},{"order":9,"type":"code","text":"data = {
    'Name': ['Alice', 'Bob', 'Charlie'],
    'Age': [25, 30, 35],
    'Active': [True, False, True]
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df)"},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"Internal Architecture and Memory Model"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"Unlike traditional relational databases or 2D NumPy arrays, a Pandas DataFrame does not store data in a single monolithic 2D memory block. Instead, it uses a dictionary-like architecture where each column is an independent Series pointing to its own memory buffer."},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Columns can have heterogeneous data types (e.g., column A is int64, column B is float64, column C is object)."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Row-based operations can sometimes be slower than column-based operations due to the column-major memory layout."},{"order":14,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Index alignment enables fast lookups and automatic data alignment during arithmetic operations."},{"order":15,"type":"subheading","text":"Inspecting Architectural Attributes"},{"order":16,"type":"paragraph","text":"You can inspect the structural attributes of any DataFrame or Series using properties like values, index, and dtypes."},{"order":17,"type":"code","text":"# Inspecting DataFrame components
print(df.values)   # Returns the underlying NumPy 2D array
print(df.index)    # Returns the Index object for rows
print(df.columns)  # Returns the Index object for columns
print(df.dtypes)   # Returns the data type of each column"},{"order":18,"type":"heading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"Mastering the Series and DataFrame architecture allows you to avoid anti-patterns like iterative row-processing and instead leverage vectorized operations built on top of NumPy."}]
